According to the Global TB Report 2021, the prevalence of smoking among men in the 10 countries with the highest TB incidence is a median of 35% (IQR: 18–45%), while among women, it is 2% (IQR: 1–3%). Tobacco use nearly doubles the risk of developing TB, with an estimated 730,000 new TB cases in 2020 attributed to tobacco use. Smoking is also associated with poor TB treatment outcomes, but implementing tobacco cessation programs can improve treatment success and reduce relapse rates. 2. Individuals with diabetes who smoke have a higher risk of developing TB compared to non-smoking diabetics, highlighting the compounded risk of multimorbidity involving diabetes and smoking. 3. To estimate the number of deaths averted by collaborative TB/HIV activities, the actual number of TB deaths can be compared to the estimated number of deaths that would have occurred without antiretroviral therapy (ART) provided alongside TB treatment for people with HIV-associated TB. These estimates are conservative as they do not account for the impact of TB services, ART availability, or TB preventive treatment on TB incidence, nor the downstream effects of these interventions on future infections, cases, and deaths. 4. The 10 countries with the highest TB incidence in 2020 were Bangladesh, China, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, India, Indonesia, Nigeria, Pakistan, the Philippines, South Africa, and Vietnam. 5. Smoking may synergistically increase the risk of TB. Since 2008, the WHO has recommended screening for tobacco use and implementing tobacco cessation activities among TB patients as part of broader tobacco control initiatives. 6. Undernutrition triples the risk of developing TB disease compared to individuals without undernutrition. Undernutrition is both a risk factor for TB and a common consequence of the disease. Lower body mass index (BMI) is consistently associated with increased TB risk and more severe lung disease. Undernutrition is also linked to poorer TB treatment outcomes and higher mortality, while weight gain during treatment predicts better outcomes. Since 2013, the WHO has recommended nutritional assessment, counseling, and co-management of TB and undernutrition, as well as TB screening among individuals with undernutrition. 7. Chronic respiratory diseases, including silicosis, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and lung cancer, are significant risk factors for TB. Silicosis increases the risk of TB fourfold, with greater severity of silicosis correlating with higher TB risk. In southern African countries, HIV is a common comorbidity among miners with silicosis, and the combination of HIV and silicosis further elevates TB risk. The WHO recommends TB screening for workers exposed to silica and preventive TB treatment for individuals with silicosis. 8. A history of TB disease is strongly associated with chronic respiratory disease in adults in TB-endemic areas. Individuals who have recovered from TB may require post-treatment care and lung rehabilitation. Strengthened collaboration between TB services and other lung disease services is critical for early diagnosis, appropriate treatment, and improved outcomes. 9. The COVID-19 pandemic has disrupted TB services globally, leading to a decline in TB case notifications. The WHO has recommended measures to maintain essential TB services during the pandemic. Evidence suggests that individuals with both COVID-19 and TB have an elevated risk of mortality. Similarly, people with HIV-associated TB are at higher risk of severe COVID-19 and higher mortality rates. Key risk factors for poor outcomes in both COVID-19 and TB include diabetes and smoking, supporting a multimorbidity approach with simultaneous screening and testing where indicated. 10. COVID-19 and TB share common transmission routes (close contact) and symptoms (cough, fever, difficulty breathing). Services should be aligned to enable rapid diagnosis, differential diagnosis, and timely treatment, with attention to infection prevention and control (IPC). 11. People with drug use disorders, whether injecting or non-injecting, are at higher risk of TB infection and disease, regardless of HIV status. TB is a leading cause of HIV-related mortality among people who inject drugs (PWID). Drug use disorders are also associated with comorbidities such as HIV, viral hepatitis, and mental disorders. Marginalization, stigma, and discrimination impede access to TB care for people who use drugs (PWUD). The WHO recommends a comprehensive package of services for PWUD, including harm reduction, TB prevention and management, and addressing structural barriers like stigma and criminalization. 12. Mental health conditions are common among people with TB, with 2% experiencing depression and elevated risks of anxiety and psychosis, particularly among those with multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB). Social stressors such as stigma, discrimination, isolation, and lack of support exacerbate mental health challenges. Integrated mental health interventions within TB services can improve treatment completion rates. The WHO recommends providing psychological support for TB patients. 13. Chronic viral hepatitis, including hepatitis B (HBV) and hepatitis C (HCV), is prevalent among populations at high risk for TB, such as PWID and incarcerated individuals. Coinfection with TB and viral hepatitis increases the risk of drug-induced liver injury during TB treatment and higher mortality rates. The WHO advises TB screening as part of the clinical evaluation for HBV and HCV treatment and recommends screening for viral hepatitis among TB patients who inject drugs. 14. Other clinical risk factors for TB include treatment with anti-tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNFα), dialysis, and organ transplantation. These conditions increase the risk of developing TB disease among those with latent TB infection. The WHO recommends systematic testing and treatment of TB infection in these high-risk groups to prevent disease progression. 15. The WHO emphasizes evidence-based, data-driven responses to TB and comorbidities. Continuous data collection and analysis are essential to identify problems, prioritize solutions, and optimize interventions. Multisectoral engagement and accountability are critical for advancing the global TB response, with clear roles and responsibilities for stakeholders and regular monitoring and evaluation. 16. People-centered services are essential for addressing TB and comorbidities, providing holistic, individualized, and empowering care. These services improve continuity of care, promote health equity, and ensure that individuals and communities are active participants in their care. A people-centered approach supports autonomy, shared decision-making, and equitable access to services, contributing to universal health coverage (UHC). 17. The WHO underscores the importance of protecting and promoting human rights, ethics, and equity in TB care. Social determinants of health, such as socioeconomic status, education, and housing, significantly influence TB risk and outcomes.
